criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water service provision and access (as well as secondary municipal sanitation access statistics) across rural and urban areas of Amathole District Municipality.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — the study examines municipal water governance and public administration processes, specifically dimensions of social equity including stakeholder participation in Integrated Development Plan (IDP) consultations, councillor accountability, municipal audit/transparency shortcomings, and intergovernmental coordination between the district and local municipalities. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: No — empirically, the study assesses generic municipal infrastructure/project delivery and operation-and-maintenance deficits (water carting, dry boreholes, uncompleted schemes) alongside broad participatory and accountability governance background (IDP roadshows, councillor visibility, audit disclaimers, intergovernmental road-building coordination), rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Policies such as Free Basic Water and the 200 m standpipe standard are mentioned only as background context and are not empirically analysed as access mechanisms.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical exploratory qualitative case study drawing on semi-structured in-depth interviews (n = 20 municipal and water-board officials/councillors), two community focus group discussions (n = 14), participant observation, and secondary municipal IDP/annual report data, analysed thematically.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative and descriptive secondary evidence on rural-urban disparities in piped water access, reliance on unsafe rivers and rainwater harvesting, inconsistent water tankering, intermittent water supply, and non-functioning boreholes and tap schemes.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (communities/households and municipal water-governance actors in Amathole District Municipality; n = 34 participants), study design (qualitative case study), governance/delivery factors examined, and service-access outcomes are clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: The purpose of this article was to explore water service provision and social equity in a rural district municipality in the Eastern Cape Province, South Africa.
Two focus group discussions were held with community members (n = 14), and semi-structured in-depth interviews (n = 20) were conducted with municipal officials involved in water service provision

Focus group discussions conducted also revealed that because of lack of access to water services, rural areas highly depend on alternative sources of water, and in most cases, these are dams and rivers, and those who feel it is not safe and clean will practice water harvesting.
The researchers examined stakeholder participation and adherence to governance principles of openness and accountability, as these are key tools used to ensure procedural fairness.

Unfortunately, the same difficulties exist in the division of powers and functions between the district and local municipalities, resulting in project implementation delays, which may be traced back to coordination and consultation shortcomings.

raw_response.exposure: Municipal water governance and social equity dimensions (IDP stakeholder consultation, councillor accountability, intergovernmental project coordination, and municipal infrastructure/water-carting delivery)
raw_response.outcome: Community and household access to safe drinking water, service consistency/intermittency, reliance on rivers or water carting, and rural-urban access disparities
raw_response.population_and_sample: Communities and municipal water-governance stakeholders in Amathole District Municipality, Eastern Cape Province, South Africa; purposeful sample of n = 34 participants (14 community members in two focus groups and 20 municipal/Water Board officials and councillors in semi-structured interviews) plus municipal IDP secondary records
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this qualitative case study empirically examines rural-urban disparities in household and community drinking-water access and reliability in South Africa's Amathole District Municipality (satisfying C1, C3, C4, C5, and C6), it does not satisfy Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification. While it meets the plain wording of Criterion 2 by discussing municipal water governance, IDP public participation, councillor accountability, and intergovernmental coordination, its empirical analysis focuses on generic project/infrastructure delivery and O&M failures (dry boreholes, insufficient water-carting trucks, stalled tap schemes) and broad participatory/accountability governance deficits rather than any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (e.g. eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariffs, enforcement, or regulatory/ownership rules).
raw_response.study_design: Exploratory qualitative case study (in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, participant observation, and secondary municipal document review)
